title: The Winter of the Ninth Floor
premise: Folklorist Odile Ashgrove arrives at Wintermere House, a decaying care home on a moor, to record the residents' songs before its sale to developers. Her overnight sleep recordings begin capturing a second voice — patient, courteous, and asking questions about 1974 — and she realizes the house itself is interviewing her. The ninth floor, sealed since a fire that year, holds the truth: the residents' memories were taken as payment for safety, and the voice is the keeper who collected them. To free the last resident, ninety-year-old Maren, from signing away what remains of her mind, Odile must climb to the ninth floor and return the stolen songs — accepting that her own memories will be the price.
about_author: Petra Halloran spent a decade cataloguing vanishing folk traditions across northern England before turning to horror, where she writes about the things communities agree not to remember. She lives near the moors and still keeps her doors counted.

chapters.title: The House That Counts Back
chapters.summary: Odile arrives at Wintermere House through freezing rain, greeted by caretaker Bram and an odd ritual: every door is counted aloud at dusk. POV Odile. The beat is uneasy wonder — she's drawn to places that keep rules, but this one seems to keep them for reasons no one will name.

chapters.title: Songs They Won't Sing Twice
chapters.summary: Odile records the residents' folk songs; each singer stops mid-verse at the same line and refuses to continue, as if the words were lifted out of them. POV Odile. The emotional beat is professional fascination curdling into dread when three residents describe the missing verses identically.

chapters.title: Maren's Empty Chair
chapters.summary: Odile befriends Maren, the last original resident from 1974, who is lucid only in fragments and keeps signing blank papers 'for the fire.' POV Maren, brief and fractured. The beat is tenderness laced with terror — Maren recognizes something in Odile and calls her by another woman's name.

chapters.title: The Ninth Floor Is Not on the Plans
chapters.summary: Bram shows Odile the building maps: eight floors, though the stairwell clearly continues upward behind a painted-shut door. POV Odile. The beat is quiet vertigo — the architecture itself is lying, and everyone treats this as normal.

chapters.title: What the Recorder Hears at Night
chapters.summary: Reviewing overnight audio, Odile finds a second voice answering questions she never asked aloud — polite, patient, asking about 1974. POV Odile. The beat is cold recognition: the house has begun its interview, and it already knows her answers.

chapters.title: The Residents' Shared Dream
chapters.summary: Several residents wake describing the same dream: a warm room above the clouds where someone sings their missing verses back to them. POV Bram. The beat is protective guilt — Bram has heard this before, in 1974, and did nothing.

chapters.title: Ledger of Small Debts
chapters.summary: In the archive, Odile finds a ledger listing residents' names beside entries like 'one summer' and 'her mother's face,' all dated 1974. POV Odile. The beat is horrified comprehension — the fire wasn't a tragedy; it was a transaction.

chapters.title: He Asks About You
chapters.summary: The night voice begins addressing Odile directly through the recorder, asking what she'd trade to belong somewhere. Lonely after years of transience, she almost answers. POV Odile. The beat is dangerous temptation — belonging offered at a price she can't yet see.

chapters.title: The Woman Called Ashgrove
chapters.summary: Maren, briefly lucid, reveals there was another folklorist in 1974 named Ashgrove who climbed to the ninth floor and never came down whole. POV Maren. The beat is shattering implication — Odile's surname is not coincidence; she was summoned, or inherited.

chapters.title: Doors Out of Count
chapters.summary: The counting ritual fails one night: thirteen doors where twelve should be. Residents wake weeping without knowing why. POV Bram. The beat is escalating panic — the house is loosening its own rules because the sale papers threaten its contract.

chapters.title: The Developer's Signature
chapters.summary: A representative arrives with final sale papers; whoever signs last dissolves the house's claim on every memory it holds — including the residents' remaining selves. POV the developer, brisk and blind. The beat is ticking-clock dread beneath banal corporate courtesy.

chapters.title: What Was Taken in 1974
chapters.summary: Piecing together testimony, Odile learns the residents traded their memories to the keeper on the ninth floor for protection from the fire — and the first folklorist, Ashgrove, tried to steal them back and was kept instead. POV Odile. The beat is grief and resolve fused into purpose.

chapters.title: The Song That Remembers Itself
chapters.summary: Maren hums a complete verse for the first time in fifty years — and the whole house goes silent to listen. POV Maren. The beat is fragile hope: a returned memory proves they can be given back.

chapters.title: Negotiating with the Dark Above
chapters.summary: Through the recorder, Odile bargains with the keeper: herself in exchange for the residents' memories. He agrees, but insists she come up and sign like everyone else. POV Odile. The beat is solemn courage shadowed by doubt about what 'herself' will mean afterward.

chapters.title: The Stairwell Opens
chapters.summary: On the winter solstice, the painted door unseals itself; warm light and the smell of a long-burned fire spill down the stairs. POV Bram, who follows her against her orders. The beat is threshold terror — the ascent neither of them may survive unchanged.

chapters.title: Ninth Floor
chapters.summary: Above the clouds lies a preserved 1974 common room where the first Ashgrove sits singing to empty chairs, half-kept, half-hollow. POV Odile. The beat is heartbreak — the keeper isn't a monster but a lonely custodian who never learned how to give anything back.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Question
chapters.summary: The keeper asks his true question: not what Odile will trade, but whether anyone ever chose to stay without being made to. She answers honestly — that belonging forced is just another theft. POV Odile. The beat is the story's moral hinge, spoken plainly in the dark.

chapters.title: Signing Back
chapters.summary: Odile reverses the ledger, entering returns instead of takings, while the first Ashgrove's song unravels the keeper's hold floor by floor. POV Odile. The beat is sacrificial climax — each returned memory takes one of hers, and she keeps writing anyway.

chapters.title: The Fire, Again, Properly
chapters.summary: The ninth floor burns at last, truly and finally, releasing fifty years of held memory back down the stairwell like migrating birds. POV Bram watching from below. The beat is cathartic release — grief and restoration arriving in the same breath.

chapters.title: What Odile Cannot Recall
chapters.summary: Odile wakes with gaps: her mother's face, her reason for coming, the sound of her own childhood. But Maren remembers everything now, and remembers her. POV Maren. The beat is bittersweet exchange — found family filling the space memory left.

chapters.title: Papers Unsigned
chapters.summary: The developer leaves without signatures; the residents vote to keep Wintermere House, doors counted, songs sung twice now, all the way through. POV Bram. The beat is hard-won peace — a community choosing to remember together rather than trade remembering away.

chapters.title: The Winter of the Ninth Floor
chapters.summary: Spring comes late. Odile stays on as Wintermere's archivist, relearning herself through the residents who carry pieces of her kindness back to her daily. On the recorder some nights, a faint voice says thank you. POV Odile. The beat is quiet resolution: belonging isn't remembered, it's practiced.
